one_liner: Header-only constexpr C++20 fixed-width big integers and Z/qZ arithmetic; beats GMP mpn_mul at 2-4 limbs.
what_it_does: ctbignum provides big_int<N, T>, a thin wrapper over std::array of limbs, plus constexpr functions for add/sub, schoolbook mul, Knuth division, Granlund-Montgomery division by invariant integers, Barrett and Montgomery reduction, modular inverse and modular exponentiation. A ZqElement type (declared via decltype(Zq(<modulus>_Z))) gives operator-overloaded arithmetic modulo a compile-time modulus, and the _Z literal parses base-10 numbers at compile time. It is a different interface from GMP: sizes and moduli are template parameters, there is no heap allocation and no dynamic growth.
how_it_is_fast: Because the limb count is a template parameter, the schoolbook loops (using unsigned __int128 for 64-bit limbs) have fixed trip counts that the compiler fully unrolls and, with [[gnu::always_inline]], inlines into the caller, avoiding GMP's call overhead and length dispatch. Arguments are passed by value so limbs can live in registers. Modulus-dependent constants for Barrett/Montgomery reduction and invariant division are precomputed at compile time.
when_to_use: Cryptographic field/ring arithmetic on 2-4 64-bit limbs (128-256 bits), e.g. elliptic-curve or pairing fields, where the modulus is known at compile time.

Tight inner loops of many small multiplications or Montgomery multiplications where GMP's per-call overhead dominates (paper: 4-limb Montgomery mul 39 ns vs libff assembly 66 ns, with forced inlining).
You want big-integer constants or precomputation evaluated at compile time (constexpr, static_assert on big-integer results).
Embedded or allocation-free code that needs fixed-size stack integers and only the C++ standard library.
when_not_to_use: Operands of about 5-6 limbs or more: GMP's mpn_mul is faster (8 limbs: 85 vs 67 ns with -march=native, 125 vs 69 ns without).
Sizes not known at compile time or numbers that grow; there is no arbitrary-precision type (fixed vs expanding separation is an open issue).
Side-channel-sensitive code that assumes every function is constant-time: the README says only explicitly marked functions are (add, mul and comparison are ct-verif checked).
MSVC builds: the code relies on __uint128_t and [[gnu::always_inline]], and MSVC support is an open issue (#44).
Large-number algorithms: multiplication is O(n^2) schoolbook only, with no Karatsuba/FFT.

integration.dependencies: none (C++ standard library); benchmarks need GMP, NTL 10.5+, libff and Google Benchmark
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (releases up to v0.3 were C++17 on Clang 5 / Apple LLVM 9); needs GCC/Clang extensions __uint128_t and gnu::always_inline
integration.platforms: 64-bit targets where the compiler provides __uint128_t (GCC/Clang on x86-64, aarch64); MSVC not supported
integration.thread_safety: Value types with no shared state; not documented explicitly
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: replaces GMP mpn/mpz only for fixed-width operands whose limb count is known at compile time; different API (big_int<N>, ZqElement)

gotchas: The headline wins assume forced inlining and -march=native; without -march=native the 2-limb gain shrinks (5 vs 13 ns) and GMP is 1.8x faster at 8 limbs.
mul returns big_int<M+N>, so result width grows by type; use partial_mul or Montgomery/Barrett reduction to stay at a fixed width.
Open bug #55: bit shifts larger than the limb bit width do not work.
ZqElement's skip_reduction constructor assumes input < modulus and does not check it.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick ctbignum over mp++ or FLINT when the width is fixed at compile time and small (2-4 limbs), or when you need constexpr evaluation; mp++/FLINT handle arbitrary sizes and grow dynamically. The AVX-512 batched Montgomery entry targets 1024-4096-bit operands in batches of 8, a different regime from ctbignum's 100-500-bit scalar operations.
verified_claims_summary: The 2018 arXiv paper times schoolbook multiplication against GMP mpn_mul on a 2.3 GHz Kaby Lake i5 (Turbo off) with Apple LLVM 9.0.0 -O3 -march=native and forced inlining: 4 vs 14 ns at 2 limbs (3.5x), 18 vs 29 ns at 4 limbs (1.6x), and 85 vs 67 ns at 8 limbs, where GMP wins. The public benchmark source is benchmarks/src/bench-mul.cpp.
status_note: Small, Apache-2.0 header-only library marked 'work in progress' in its README, with commits as recent as 2026-08-07 and 12 open issues; easy to vendor, though the published benchmarks date from 2018.
